entries.question: Abram casts [Lightning Bolt] targeting Nola. As it resolves, can Abram choose to deal the damage to Nola's [Vivien Reid]?

votes.reason: Both answers correctly state that Lightning Bolt cannot be redirected to a planeswalker.

entries.reason: Both answers correctly state that Lightning Bolt cannot be redirected to a planeswalker.
entries.answer:
No. Lightning Bolt deals 3 damage to Nola, and Abram cannot switch that damage to Nola's Vivien Reid on resolution.

Two reasons:

1. The old planeswalker redirection rule no longer exists. Under the current rules, a player can no longer choose to have noncombat damage that would be dealt to an opponent be dealt to a planeswalker that opponent controls instead; that rule was removed, and cards that still do this were given Oracle errata to deal damage directly to planeswalkers [306.7]. Lightning Bolt's text is simply "Lightning Bolt deals 3 damage to any target," with no redirection clause.

2. The target is locked in when the spell is cast, not chosen at resolution. Lightning Bolt says "any target," which may be a creature, player, planeswalker, or battle [115.4]. Abram chose Nola as that target when casting, and only an effect that specifically changes targets or chooses new targets can alter it [115.7b]. Redirection effects (a kind of replacement effect that moves damage from one creature, planeswalker, or player to another) exist, but only if some spell or ability actually creates one, such as a card that says the next X damage to one target is dealt to another target instead [614.9, Redirection Effect]. Neither Lightning Bolt nor Vivien Reid provides such an effect.

If Abram wants to damage Vivien Reid, he must target Vivien Reid with Lightning Bolt in the first place, which rule 115.4 permits since planeswalkers are legal choices for "any target."

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more than two; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Lightning Bolt deals damage to its target, Nola. There is no rule that allows damage dealt to a player to be redirected to a planeswalker.

entries.answer:
Samurai of the Pale Curtain moves from the battlefield to Anthony's graveyard.

Why: a face-down permanent is a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no mana cost, and no abilities. That means the face-down Samurai of the Pale Curtain has neither its Bushido 1 ability nor its own replacement ability ("If a permanent would be put into a graveyard, exile it instead") while it's face down, so nothing redirects it to exile. Embereth Shieldbreaker (2/1) deals 2 combat damage to the face-down 2/2, which is lethal, and it's put into the graveyard as a state-based action.

As Samurai of the Pale Curtain leaves the battlefield face down, Anthony must reveal it to all players as he moves it to the graveyard [708.9]; once in the graveyard it's simply the face-up card Samurai of the Pale Curtain. Note that its own exile-replacement effect only functions from the battlefield while face up, so it can't save itself here.

Meanwhile Embereth Shieldbreaker (a 2/1) also takes 2 damage from the face-down creature and is destroyed, going to Noemi's graveyard — the face-down Samurai of the Pale Curtain's replacement effect isn't active to exile it instead.

This is unaffected by player count: the blocking and damage interaction plays out identically at a two-player or multiplayer table.

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming ordinary combat damage in the combat damage step, with Samurai of the Pale Curtain still face down when damage is dealt. If Anthony turns it face up (by paying a morph/disguise-style cost) before combat damage, it would be a 2/2 Samurai of the Pale Curtain with Bushido 1 (becoming 3/3 after being blocked), it would survive, Embereth Shieldbreaker would be exiled instead of going to the graveyard, and nothing would move to a graveyard.

entries.answer_gold: The graveyard. Replacement effects must exist before the event in question in order to affect it. Samurai of the Pale Curtain had no abilities when it was on the battlefield, so there is no replacement effect that would apply to it moving to the graveyard.

entries.question: Addison casts [Ferocious Zheng]. After it resolves, they cast [Elemental Eruption] and reveal [Everdream] from their hand, splicing it onto Elemental Eruption. When Elemental Eruption's Storm trigger resolves, will the copies of Elemental Eruption also have Everdream spliced onto them?

votes.reason: The candidate correctly states that the copies of Elemental Eruption will have Everdream spliced onto them because choices made during casting are copied.

entries.answer:
Yes. The copy of Elemental Eruption created by its storm ability will have Everdream's text spliced onto it, so it also draws Addison a card.

Why: splicing is a choice made while casting Elemental Eruption, and copying a spell copies both its characteristics and all decisions made for it [707.10]. Everdream's own ruling states this directly: "If a spell is copied, choices made while casting it are copied, so the copy will have the same abilities spliced onto it as the original" [Everdream ruling #4]. Splice works by adding Everdream's rules text to Elemental Eruption as a text-changing effect [702.47c, 612.10], and that added text resolves after Elemental Eruption's own effect [Everdream ruling #1, 702.47b].

Storm count here: storm copies the spell for each other spell cast before it this turn [702.40a]. Ferocious Zheng was cast this turn, so there's exactly 1 copy. Revealing and paying for Everdream via splice is not casting Everdream, so it does not add to the storm count. Net result: Elemental Eruption plus one copy resolve, creating two 4/4 red Dragon Elemental tokens with flying and prowess and drawing two cards total.

A couple of notes: the copy is put directly onto the stack and isn't cast, so it won't be counted by later storm spells [Elemental Eruption ruling #2, 707.10]. The copy is also still a red sorcery — splice doesn't give it Everdream's name, mana cost, or color [702.47c]. The storm copy resolves before the original Elemental Eruption, since copies go on the stack above it [608.1].

Multiplayer: nothing here changes with more than two players — storm counts all spells cast by any player this turn, and the splice-copying rule is unaffected by player count.

entries.answer_gold: Yes. As Addison is casting Elemental Eruption they choose whether they want to splice as part of the casting process. When the storm trigger resolves it copies all the choices made when casting the original spell, including the choice to splice.

entries.answer:
It enters the battlefield tapped.

Why: Vesuva's ability is a replacement effect that modifies how it enters — "You may have this land enter tapped as a copy of any land on the battlefield." When several replacement effects want to modify the same enters-the-battlefield event, and one of them would make the object a copy of something, that copy effect must be chosen and applied first [616.1c], [616.1f]. So Adrien applies Vesuva's copy effect first: Vesuva enters as a copy of Urban Retreat, which means it also copies Urban Retreat's name and its printed ability "This land enters tapped" [707.5], [Vesuva ruling #0], [Vesuva ruling #3].

Now you re-check which other replacement effects apply, using the permanent's characteristics as it would exist on the battlefield after the effects already applied [614.12]. At that point the land's name is Urban Retreat, not Vesuva, so Nylah's Alpine Moon — which only affects "lands your opponents control with the chosen name" (Vesuva) — simply doesn't apply to it. Alpine Moon never strips the "enters tapped" ability, so both Vesuva's own "enter tapped" clause and the copied Urban Retreat ability leave it tapped.

Contrast: if Adrien's Vesuva were entering without copying anything (no land chosen), it would still be named Vesuva, Alpine Moon would apply and strip its land types and abilities, and it would enter untapped as a land that only has "{T}: Add one mana of any color" [Alpine Moon ruling #0], [Vesuva ruling #2].

Assumption: Adrien is an opponent of Nylah's (Alpine Moon only affects opponents' lands). This works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table — the only thing that changes with more players is that simultaneous choices are made in APNAP order [101.4].

entries.answer_gold: This can't happen as described. Adrien cannot choose a land to copy with Vesuva because it loses that ability before it would apply. Vesuva enters untapped, as itself.

entries.answer:
Yes — Ares can still choose a multicolored card with Glittering Wish.

Why: Mycosynth Lattice's second ability says "All cards that aren't on the battlefield, spells, and permanents are colorless," and its ruling clarifies that this makes everything colorless "in every zone of the game" [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #2]. Cards outside the game — such as those in Ares's sideboard — are not in any of the game's zones; outside the game is not a zone at all [400.11a], and sideboard cards are outside the game [400.11a, 100.4]. So Mycosynth Lattice's color-changing effect doesn't reach them, and a multicolored card in Ares's sideboard is still multicolored when Glittering Wish resolves and asks him to reveal "a multicolored card you own from outside the game."

Once that card is revealed and put into Ares's hand, it is then in a game zone and Mycosynth Lattice makes it colorless from that point on — but that happens after the choice, so it doesn't stop Glittering Wish from finding it.

Note also that Glittering Wish says "may," so Ares is never forced to find one, and searching/finding from outside the game is a matter of choosing an appropriate card he owns [701.23j].

This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

No. The Twin token created by Gemini Engine enters the battlefield untapped, and attacking. Gemini Engine's ability says only that the token is created "attacking" — it says nothing about the token being tapped, and a token has no characteristics or status other than what the creating ability defines [111.3]. Permanents enter the battlefield untapped, unflipped, face up, and phased in unless a spell or ability says otherwise [110.5b], and Gemini Engine doesn't say otherwise. This is confirmed directly by the ruling: "The Twin token enters as an untapped attacking creature. It's not subject to any costs to attack or restrictions on attacking" [Gemini Engine ruling #3].

Note that attacking and being tapped are separate things — creatures are normally tapped as a cost of being declared as attackers, but a token put onto the battlefield already attacking skips the declare-attackers process entirely, so it is never tapped. This means the Twin can still be tapped later for an effect that requires tapping an untapped creature.

One caveat: an outside effect such as a permanent that reads "Permanents enter tapped" would be a replacement effect modifying how the token enters [614.1c], [614.12], and would make the Twin enter tapped; also, since a replacement effect applying to a token entering the battlefield is applied after continuous effects that modify its characteristics [701.7b]. Absent such an effect, the Twin is untapped. This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more than two; Gemini Engine's ability affects only its controller's own token.

entries.answer:
Yes — Skull Prophet returns to the battlefield when Baylor becomes the monarch by dealing combat damage to Carolyn.

Why: Because Consign to Memory countered Palace Jailer's first triggered ability, Alexis never became the monarch; Carolyn stayed the monarch. Per [Palace Jailer ruling #6], when Palace Jailer's second ability resolves while its controller (Alexis) is not the monarch, Skull Prophet is exiled until there is a *new* monarch and that new monarch is one of Alexis's opponents — Carolyn already being the monarch does not immediately bring Skull Prophet back.

Being the monarch carries the inherent triggered ability "Whenever a creature deals combat damage to the monarch, its controller becomes the monarch" [725.2], [Palace Jailer ruling #1]. So when Baylor's creature deals combat damage to Carolyn, Baylor becomes the monarch. Baylor is an opponent of Alexis, which satisfies the exile duration; it does not matter that Baylor is also the exiled card's owner — any opponent becoming the monarch causes the return [Palace Jailer ruling #5]. The one-shot exile effect "until" that event ends, and a second one-shot effect immediately returns the card to the battlefield under its owner's control, i.e., Baylor's [610.3c].

Notes: this scenario is inherently multiplayer (Alexis, Baylor, Carolyn), and the monarch rules used here apply the same regardless of player count; with only two players there'd simply be no third player to hold the monarchy. Also, Palace Jailer leaving the battlefield would not bring Skull Prophet back — the game keeps watching for the next time an opponent becomes the monarch [Palace Jailer ruling #3].

entries.answer_gold: Yes. When Palace Jailer's second triggered ability resolves it has a duration that expires when the monarch changes to an opponent.

Note the replacement lasts the whole turn, not just for the damage itself: per Touch of the Void ruling #4, once Orzhov Racketeers has been dealt damage by Touch of the Void, if it would die for any reason later that turn (another burn spell, a -X/-X effect, a sacrifice-free destruction, etc.), it's exiled instead — so afterlife stays shut off for the rest of the turn. If Orzhov Racketeers somehow leaves the battlefield and returns, it's a new object with no memory of its previous existence (rule 400.7), so the exile-replacement no longer applies to it and afterlife could work normally.

One timing caveat: this assumes Touch of the Void's damage is what causes Orzhov Racketeers to die. entries.answer:
Yes — Abdullah can block Walking Corpse with Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker, provided Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker is untapped.

Why: only creatures can block, and after Liquimetal Coating and Karn, the Great Creator's +1 ability, Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker is an artifact creature (with power and toughness each equal to its mana value, 8, so an 8/8) that is still also a planeswalker [506.3, 302.5]. When declaring blockers, Abdullah chooses untapped creatures he controls that aren't battles, and each may block a creature that's attacking Abdullah, a planeswalker Abdullah controls, or a battle Abdullah protects [509.1, 509.1a]. Walking Corpse is attacking Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker, which is a planeswalker Abdullah controls, so Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker legally blocks the very creature attacking it.

After the block, Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker is simultaneously a blocking creature and a planeswalker that's being attacked. It stays in combat in both roles; it would only be removed from combat entirely if it stopped being both a creature and a planeswalker. If it stops being just one of those types (for example, Karn, the Great Creator's animation ending), it continues in the other role — still a blocking creature, or still a planeswalker being attacked, whichever applies [506.4d]. Note also that Karn, the Great Creator's +1 required a *noncreature* artifact as its target, which is why the Liquimetal Coating activation had to come first.

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming Liquimetal Coating resolved before Karn, the Great Creator's +1 was activated (as stated) and that both effects are still in place when blockers are declared. If the animation from Karn, the Great Creator had already ended before the declare blockers step, Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker would be a noncreature permanent and could not block at all [506.3].

On the combat damage itself: the rules supplied here cover legality of the block, not how combat damage is dealt to a permanent that is both a creature and a planeswalker, so I won't state loyalty-versus-damage specifics — that portion isn't in the provided context.

Multiplayer: with more than two players, the same answer holds; each defending player declares blockers in APNAP order and may block only creatures attacking that player, a planeswalker they control, or a battle they protect [802.4a, 101.4]. Under the shared team turns option the defending team makes one combined legal block instead [805.10d].

entries.answer_gold:
Yes, any creature controlled by the defending player can block an attacker. Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker will be dealt 2 damage, resulting in 2 damage being marked on it and it losing two loyalty counters.

Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker is still a planeswalker. Effects that make a permanent an 'artifact creature' allow that permanent to retain its other types. Damage dealt to Nicol Bolas, Planeswalker will still result in loyalty counters being removed from it.

entries.answer:
No. Volunteer Militia still can't attack.

Two independent reasons:

1. Opportunistic Dragon's ability doesn't just remove abilities — it says "For as long as this creature remains on the battlefield, gain control of that permanent, it loses all abilities, and it can't attack or block." The "can't attack or block" part is a separate continuous restriction, not an ability of Volunteer Militia, so making Volunteer Militia lose all abilities with Oko, Thief of Crowns' +1 does nothing to it. Oko, Thief of Crowns' +1 only overwrites abilities, colors, types, and P/T; effects that add or remove abilities are a distinct thing from restriction effects [113.10, 113.10b]. And a "can't" effect beats anything that would allow the attack [101.2a]. Opportunistic Dragon's printed text controls here over any general expectation that stripping abilities clears restrictions. The card ruling confirms the restriction sticks even through later control changes [Opportunistic Dragon ruling #0].

2. Even ignoring that, Adrian gained control of Volunteer Militia this turn, so on the turn it was stolen it also couldn't attack under the summoning sickness rule — a creature can't attack unless it has been under its controller's control continuously since that player's most recent turn began [302.6], and Volunteer Militia has no haste [702.10b]. Note Oko, Thief of Crowns' +1 also strips any abilities, so it certainly won't grant haste.

The restriction lasts for as long as Opportunistic Dragon remains on the battlefield [611.2b]. If Opportunistic Dragon leaves the battlefield, Adrian loses control of Volunteer Militia (it goes back to Natalia) and the "can't attack or block" ends — but Volunteer Militia would still be a 3/3 Elk with no abilities from Oko, Thief of Crowns, since that effect has no duration tied to Opportunistic Dragon. Also, if Opportunistic Dragon had left the battlefield before its trigger resolved, Adrian would never have gained control at all [Opportunistic Dragon ruling #3].

This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games; nothing here depends on the number of players, other than that Opportunistic Dragon's trigger targets a Human or artifact an opponent controls.

entries.answer_gold: No. Opportunistic Dragon does not grant an ability to Volunteer Militia that prevents it from attacking. Instead its trigger creates an effect that states that Volunteer Militia cannot attack or block as long as Opportunistic Dragon is on the battlefield.

entries.answer:
Total damage to Neil: 8 — assuming both attackers are unblocked and Amber's life total isn't changed by anything else.

Step by step:

1. Amber is at 2 life, so Gavony Ironwright's fateful hour ability is active ("As long as you have 5 or less life, other creatures you control get +1/+4"). That buffs Drogskol Reaver to 4/9; Gavony Ironwright itself is unaffected by its own ability, so it stays 1/4.
2. First-strike combat damage step: Drogskol Reaver has double strike, so it deals damage here. It deals damage equal to its power, 4, to Neil [510.1a, 120.2a, 208.1]. Gavony Ironwright, which has no first strike, deals nothing yet.
3. Drogskol Reaver has lifelink, so Amber gains 4 life, going from 2 to 6. (That life gain also triggers Drogskol Reaver's last ability to draw a card.) Because Amber now has more than 5 life, Gavony Ironwright's fateful hour ability stops applying, and Drogskol Reaver reverts to 3/5.
4. Regular combat damage step: Drogskol Reaver deals 3 (its now-unbuffed power) and Gavony Ironwright deals 1, for 4 more damage to Neil [510.1a].

4 + 3 + 1 = 8 damage dealt to Neil. Amber ends up gaining 4 (first strike) + 3 (regular) = 7 life total from lifelink, drawing a card for each of those two life-gain events [Drogskol Reaver ruling #1].

If instead either attacker were blocked, that creature's damage would go to the blocking creature(s) rather than to Neil, so less (or no) damage would reach Neil [510.1c]. This answer is framed for Neil being the single defending player; in a multiplayer game each attacking creature would still deal its damage only to whatever player, planeswalker, or battle it was attacking.

entries.answer_gold: 8. Since a creature with double strike is attacking, there are two combat damage steps. In the first one, Drogskol Reaver deals 4 damage to Neil. entries.answer:
No. Selvala, Heart of the Wilds's ability does not trigger when Catacomb Slug enters the battlefield, because Tocatli Honor Guard says "Creatures entering don't cause abilities to trigger." That printed text overrides the general enters-the-battlefield trigger rule (603.6a), and it shuts off not just the entering creature's own ETB triggers but any triggered ability that would trigger on a creature entering — including Selvala, Heart of the Wilds's "Whenever another creature enters" ability [Tocatli Honor Guard ruling #1].

A couple of secondary points:
- Even without Tocatli Honor Guard, Selvala, Heart of the Wilds's ability only lets you draw if the entering creature's power is greater than each other creature's power; Catacomb Slug is 2/6, and Selvala, Heart of the Wilds is 2/3, so the power condition would fail anyway. But note that condition is part of the effect ("may draw a card if..."), so with Tocatli Honor Guard out the point is moot — the ability never triggers at all.
- If Tocatli Honor Guard itself and another creature entered simultaneously, neither entry would cause triggers [Tocatli Honor Guard ruling #3].
- Static "as this enters" / "enters tapped" effects are not triggered abilities (603.6d, 614.1c), so Tocatli Honor Guard would not stop those.

This answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table: Tocatli Honor Guard's ability isn't limited to its controller's creatures, so no player's creature entering causes abilities to trigger while it's on the battlefield.

The resulting merged permanent is face down and is a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no card types beyond creature, no subtypes, no abilities, and no mana cost — i.e. it looks exactly like the manifested creature did, even though Trumpeting Gnarr is now part of it.

Why: mutate makes the spell merge with the target rather than enter the battlefield, and the controller picks top or bottom (702.140c, 608.3d, 730.1). When components are merged, the permanent's status (including face up/face down) is set by its topmost component (730.2e), and here the topmost component is the manifested card, which is face down. Manifest's characteristic-defining effect makes that card a 2/2 face-down creature with no text, name, subtypes, or mana cost, and that effect keeps working as long as it's face down (701.40a). So while 702.140e would normally give the mutated permanent the abilities of every component and the other characteristics of the topmost component, the face-down state means the permanent shows only the 2/2 no-text profile — the same result as the face-down-copy examples in 707.3.

Practical consequences:
- Trumpeting Gnarr's mutate trigger ("Whenever this creature mutates, create a 3/3 green Beast creature token") is not an ability the permanent has while it's face down, so no Beast token is created. (Rules provided don't spell this out beyond 702.140e/701.40a/707.3, so treat this as the reading those rules support.)
- The target was legal: a face-down manifested creature has no subtypes, so it is a non-Human creature you own, and the spell merges instead of entering separately (702.140b would only apply on an illegal target).
- You can still turn it face up later as a special action any time you have priority, by showing that the card representing it is a creature card and paying that card's mana cost (701.40b, 116.2b). If the manifested card is not a creature card or has no mana cost, it can't be turned face up that way. If a merged face-down permanent contains an instant or sorcery card, it can't be turned face up at all (730.2g). Once it is face up, the permanent's characteristics come from the topmost card with the abilities of all components (702.140e).
- If instead Avery had put Trumpeting Gnarr on top, the topmost component would be face up, so the permanent would be a face-up 3/3 green Beast named Trumpeting Gnarr with the mutate trigger and would have created the token.

Timing note: I'm assuming the manifest resolved fully before Trumpeting Gnarr was cast, as stated; that's the only order that makes the manifested creature a legal target.

entries.answer:
Yes — Alex may cast Fires of Undeath, and this time it goes to Alex's graveyard as it resolves (not exile).

Details:

1) Casting it. Spell Queller's leaves-the-battlefield trigger says the exiled card's owner may cast that card without paying its mana cost. Alex must cast it right then, as part of that trigger's resolution — Alex can't hold it to cast later in the turn — and timing permissions based on card type are ignored (Fires of Undeath is an instant anyway) [Spell Queller ruling #1]. Alex casts it from the exile zone, putting it on the stack [112.1], [601.2b].

2) Why it isn't exiled again. Flashback means "you may cast this card from your graveyard by paying [cost] rather than its mana cost" and "if the flashback cost was paid, exile this card instead of putting it anywhere else any time it would leave the stack" [Fires of Undeath ruling #3]. That replacement applied to the earlier spell, and it's why exiling it with Spell Queller stuck [Fires of Undeath ruling #5]. But once the card changed zones it became a new object with no memory of its previous existence [400.7k], and the new spell Alex casts has no relation to the original — choices and effects affecting the original spell don't carry over [Spell Queller ruling #0]. Alex is casting it from exile for Spell Queller's alternative cost of nothing, not paying a flashback cost, so no flashback replacement is active. It resolves normally and is put into its owner's graveyard.

3) If Alex declines to cast it, or if it's countered or otherwise leaves the stack, it simply goes to Alex's graveyard for the same reason (no flashback cost was paid for this casting).

Timing note: this assumes Spell Queller's enters-the-battlefield ability already resolved and actually exiled Fires of Undeath before Spell Queller died. If Spell Queller had left the battlefield before that ability resolved, the leaves-the-battlefield trigger would resolve first and do nothing, and then Fires of Undeath would be exiled forever with no chance to cast it [Spell Queller ruling #4].

Multiplayer: nothing here changes with more than two players — the card's owner (Alex) is the one who gets the option, regardless of table size.

Because a triggered ability triggered during the process, that ability goes on the stack during the cleanup step, then the active player gets priority and players may cast spells and activate abilities [724.1f][514.3][514.3a]. At that point Aspen could cast an instant, but only by producing mana then — and Vault of Catlacan is already tapped from making the 8 blue, so it can't be tapped again for {U}. Mentor is a triggered ability: "Whenever this creature attacks, put a +1/+1 counter on target attacking creature with power less than this creature's power" [702.134a]. Triggers resolve last-on-first-off, so the resolution order is the reverse of the order given, and each check of "lesser power" is made again on resolution (if the target's power is no longer less, nothing happens) [Barging Sergeant ruling #2].

1. Barging Sergeant (4 power) targeting Tajic, Legion's Edge (3 power): legal, Tajic, Legion's Edge becomes 4/3.
2. Light of the Legion (5 power) targeting Wojek Bodyguard (3 power): legal, Wojek Bodyguard becomes 4/4.
3. Tajic, Legion's Edge (now 4 power) targeting Goblin Banneret (1 power): legal, Goblin Banneret becomes 2/2.
4. Wojek Bodyguard (now 4 power) targeting Sunhome Stalwart (2 power): legal, Sunhome Stalwart becomes 3/3.
5. Sunhome Stalwart (now 3 power) targeting Goblin Banneret (now 2 power): still lesser, so legal — Goblin Banneret becomes 3/3.

Final powers when combat damage is assigned: Goblin Banneret 3, Sunhome Stalwart 3, Tajic, Legion's Edge 4, Wojek Bodyguard 4, Barging Sergeant 4, Light of the Legion 5. Each unblocked attacker assigns damage equal to its power [510.1a], so 3+3+4+4+4+5 = 23 to Nico.

Sunhome Stalwart has first strike, so its 3 damage is dealt in the first-strike combat damage step and the other 20 in the regular step — the total is unchanged. If Nico blocks anything, that creature's damage goes to the blockers instead [510.1c]. In a multiplayer game the same math applies; Nico simply must be the defending player (or planeswalker/battle controller) all six creatures are attacking for all 23 to land on Nico.

entries.answer:
No. Azariah can't begin casting the second Demon of Catastrophes while the first Demon of Catastrophes is on the battlefield under anyone's control.

Why: Cornered Market says "Players can't cast spells with the same name as a nontoken permanent." Whether a player may begin casting a spell is checked before any of the casting steps happen — a player can begin to cast a spell only if no rule or effect prohibits it [601.3]. At that moment the first Demon of Catastrophes is still a nontoken permanent on the battlefield, so the prohibition applies and casting can never start.

The additional cost doesn't help, because it's paid far too late in the sequence. Demon of Catastrophes reads "As an additional cost to cast this spell, sacrifice a creature"; you announce your intent to pay additional costs during proposal [601.2b], the total cost is locked in at [601.2f], and the actual sacrifice happens only when you pay the total cost [601.2h], moving the permanent from the battlefield to its owner's graveyard [701.21a]. All of that is after the legality check in [601.3], so the first Demon of Catastrophes is still on the battlefield when the game asks whether the second Demon of Catastrophes may be cast. Rule [601.5] lets you take later cost-payment choices into account when choosing targets/divisions, but it does not let a planned sacrifice retroactively make an otherwise prohibited cast legal. And note that Demon of Catastrophes' sacrifice is mandatory — you can't cast it without sacrificing a creature [Demon of Catastrophes ruling #0].

What Azariah can do: get rid of the first Demon of Catastrophes first by some other means (e.g., sacrificing it to an unrelated sacrifice outlet or another spell's additional cost), so that no nontoken permanent named Demon of Catastrophes exists when the second one is proposed; then Cornered Market no longer prohibits the cast, and Azariah can cast it sacrificing some other creature. Note also that each payment applies to only one spell or ability, so one creature can't pay two sacrifice costs [118.10].

If Azariah somehow did start the cast illegally, the action is reversed and all payments are canceled [733.1].

This answer is the same regardless of player count: Cornered Market looks at nontoken permanents on the battlefield generally, so it applies whether the duplicate Demon of Catastrophes is controlled by Azariah, Nico, or a third player at a multiplayer table. Also note Cornered Market only stops casting, not effects that put cards onto the battlefield [Cornered Market ruling #1], and it looks only at permanents, not spells on the stack [Cornered Market ruling #0].

entries.answer_gold: No. Azariah can't begin casting the second Demon of Catastrophes while they still control another Demon of Catastrophes.

No — Alex can't legally declare both Gaea's Liege and Rhonas the Indomitable as attackers in this situation.

Why: Rhonas the Indomitable has the printed restriction "Rhonas can't attack or block unless you control another creature with power 4 or greater." That's a restriction checked during the declaration of attackers [508.1c]; if it's disobeyed, the whole declaration is illegal and the game rewinds to before it [508.1, 733.1]. Alex's only other creature is Gaea's Liege, whose printed text says that as long as it isn't attacking its power and toughness each equal the number of Forests Alex controls — that's 1 Forest, so Gaea's Liege is 1/1 at the time the restriction is checked. Its 5/5 size (Natalie's 5 Forests) only applies while it is attacking, so it can't retroactively satisfy Rhonas the Indomitable's requirement at declaration time. Note that Rhonas the Indomitable does not require the other creature to attack — only that Alex control it [Rhonas the Indomitable ruling #0] — but it still must have power 4 or greater.

So Alex may attack with Gaea's Liege alone (it will be 5/5 while attacking, since Natalie controls 5 Forests), but Rhonas the Indomitable can't be declared as an attacker.

Timing note: I'm assuming the restriction is checked with Gaea's Liege not yet attacking (its power 1), which is how the declaration steps read — creatures are chosen, then restrictions are checked, then the creatures are tapped [508.1a, 508.1c, 508.1f]. If one instead evaluated legality using the post-declaration state, Gaea's Liege would be 5/5 and Rhonas the Indomitable's restriction would be satisfied; the provided rules give no rule making that circular reading correct.

How to fix it before combat: Alex can activate Gaea's Liege's "{T}: Target land becomes a Forest" — but tapping Gaea's Liege means it can't be declared as an attacker at all [508.1a]. Turning Alex's own lands into Forests (via some other means) to reach 4+ Forests would make Gaea's Liege power 4 or greater while not attacking and let Rhonas the Indomitable attack.

Multiplayer: this answer doesn't change with more than two players — the same restriction check applies, and Alex would just choose which defending player, planeswalker, or battle Gaea's Liege attacks. (Under shared-team-turns rules the active team's attack must be legal as a whole [805.10b].)

entries.question: Nova controls a [Grafdigger's Cage]. Aspen controls a [Trained Orgg] and has an [Undead Minotaur] in their graveyard. Aspen casts [Stormcaller's Boon], cascading into [Living End]. What happens?

entries.answer:
Living End resolves fully and Grafdigger's Cage doesn't stop any of it. Aspen sacrifices Trained Orgg, and Undead Minotaur comes back onto the battlefield under Aspen's control.

Why Grafdigger's Cage doesn't matter here:

1. Casting: Grafdigger's Cage stops players from casting spells from graveyards or libraries. Cascade from Stormcaller's Boon exiles cards off the top of the library and lets you cast the exiled card — Living End is cast from the exile zone, not from the library, so Grafdigger's Cage permits it.

2. Entering the battlefield: Grafdigger's Cage only stops creature cards *in graveyards and libraries* from entering the battlefield. Living End first exiles all creature cards from graveyards, and only afterwards puts those exiled cards onto the battlefield. By the time Undead Minotaur is being put onto the battlefield, it is in exile, not in a graveyard, so Grafdigger's Cage's restriction doesn't apply to it.

Order of events within Living End's resolution, per its ruling: every player exiles their graveyard creature cards simultaneously, then every player sacrifices all creatures they control simultaneously (Trained Orgg dies here — and note it goes to Aspen's graveyard after the exile step, so it does not come back), then everyone puts their exiled cards onto the battlefield simultaneously. So Undead Minotaur returns, Trained Orgg does not.

Multiplayer note: Living End affects each player, so with more than two players every player exiles, sacrifices, and returns creatures in those same simultaneous steps; Grafdigger's Cage likewise fails to stop any of their returns for the same reason. Nova gets nothing out of Grafdigger's Cage in this exchange.

entries.answer_gold: Cascade casts the Living End from exile, so Grafdigger's Cage doesn't prevent it from being cast. The Living End will also resolve normally- Grafdigger's Cage only prevents creature cards from entering the battlefield from the graveyard or library. Living End puts them onto the battlefield from exile.

Why the pieces fit together:

1. Sakashima the Impostor copied Psychic Battle. Psychic Battle is a non‑Aura enchantment, and Opalescence makes each other non‑Aura enchantment a creature in addition to its other types with base power and toughness equal to its mana value — that's what let Sakashima the Impostor (which copies "any creature on the battlefield") copy it. The copy keeps Psychic Battle's copiable characteristics (enchantment, mana cost {3}{U}{U}) but is named Sakashima the Impostor and is legendary; it's still an enchantment for Opalescence's purposes, so Opalescence makes it a creature too, base 5/5 (mana value 5). An object with more than one card type combines the aspects of each and is subject to anything affecting either type (300.2, 205.2b). Note Opalescence says "each other," so Opalescence doesn't animate itself.

2. Healing Leaves requires a target in either mode ("target player gains 3 life" or prevent 3 damage to "any target"). Targets are chosen as part of casting, when the spell is put on the stack (601.2c, 115.1b). At that moment Sakashima the Impostor's copied Psychic Battle ability triggers; because it triggered during casting, it waits and is put on the stack after Healing Leaves has finished being cast, so it's above Healing Leaves and resolves first.

3. On resolution of that trigger, every player reveals their top card. The player revealing the greatest mana value may change Healing Leaves' target — normally targets can't be changed, but this effect explicitly says it can (115.1b). If two or more cards tie for greatest mana value, the target stays on Nico. Any new target must still be legal for the mode chosen: a player for the life‑gain mode, or a creature, player, planeswalker, or battle for the "any target" prevention mode (Any Target, 115.4).

4. Psychic Battle's own text says changing targets this way doesn't trigger abilities of permanents named Psychic Battle. Your permanent is named Sakashima the Impostor, not Psychic Battle, so that exclusion doesn't cover it — card text controls here, and a target change made this way is itself a choice of targets that can trigger the ability again (potentially repeatedly, each time putting a new trigger on the stack).

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming the target for Healing Leaves was announced during casting (the only legal time). Two‑player vs. multiplayer: the process is identical, but with more than two players every player at the table reveals, so ties for greatest mana value (which lock the target in place) and the identity of the player who gets to redirect can differ; with exactly two players it's simply whoever of the two reveals the higher mana value.

entries.answer:
Yes — provided Ada hasn't already cast a nonartifact spell this turn, and both actions happen in one of Ada's main phases with an empty stack. Ada can suspend Shade of Trokair and then still cast Divination.

Why:

1. Suspending is a special action, not casting. Exiling a card with suspend doesn't use the stack and isn't casting that card [116.2f] [702.62a] [Shade of Trokair ruling #7]. So Shade of Trokair does not count as a "nonartifact spell cast this turn" for Ethersworn Canonist, and it doesn't lock Ada out of casting Divination.

2. But the suspend action itself requires legality to cast. Ada may only take that special action if they could begin to cast Shade of Trokair from their hand at that moment, taking into account any effect that prohibits casting it [116.2f] [702.62c] [601.3] [Shade of Trokair ruling #2]. Ethersworn Canonist says "Each player who has cast a nonartifact spell this turn can't cast additional nonartifact spells." So:
   - If Ada has cast no nonartifact spell yet this turn, nothing prohibits casting Shade of Trokair (a creature card, so sorcery-speed timing: Ada's main phase, stack empty), and the suspend action is legal. entries.question: Alan controls [Iroas, God of Victory] and 3 other enchantments. Their devotion to white is 2. They cast [Starfield of Nyx]. After it resolves, is Iroas, God of Victory a creature? If so, what are its power and toughness?

entries.answer:
Yes — after Starfield of Nyx resolves, Iroas, God of Victory is a 4/4 creature (in addition to being a legendary enchantment).

Why Iroas, God of Victory counts for Starfield of Nyx: Alan controls Iroas, God of Victory plus 3 other enchantments plus Starfield of Nyx itself = five enchantments, so Starfield of Nyx's ability turns on. Iroas, God of Victory is a non-Aura enchantment other than Starfield of Nyx, so it's affected.

The type fight (layer 4): two continuous effects both apply in layer 4 — Iroas, God of Victory's own "As long as your devotion to red and white is less than seven, Iroas isn't a creature" and Starfield of Nyx's "is a creature in addition to its other types." Neither effect changes what the other depends on (Starfield of Nyx doesn't alter devotion), so no dependency exists and they're applied in timestamp order (613.7, 613.8). Iroas, God of Victory was already on the battlefield, so Starfield of Nyx's effect has the later timestamp and is applied last: Iroas, God of Victory ends up a creature. Note that "in addition to its other types" means it keeps enchantment (and its legendary supertype and God subtype) as well (205.1b, 205.4b).

Power and toughness (layer 7b): Starfield of Nyx sets base power and base toughness each equal to mana value. Iroas, God of Victory's mana cost is {2}{R}{W}, so its mana value is 4 — a base 4/4, replacing the printed 7/4. Applying an effect in one layer and a P/T-setting part in another to the same object is exactly the layered behavior described in 613.6, and the result is instantaneous (613.5). Any +1/+1 counters or pump effects would then apply on top in layer 7c; here there are none, so it's 4/4.

Assumption on devotion: you gave devotion to white as 2; devotion to red and white together is presumably still less than seven (Iroas, God of Victory's own {R}{W} contributes 2, and Starfield of Nyx's {W} contributes 1). That makes Iroas, God of Victory's "isn't a creature" clause active — but it loses to Starfield of Nyx's later timestamp anyway. If devotion to red and white were seven or more, Iroas, God of Victory would be a creature regardless, and Starfield of Nyx would still set it to base 4/4.

Player count doesn't matter here: devotion counts only permanents Alan controls, and nothing in this interaction involves opponents, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

entries.answer_gold:
Iroas, God of Victory is a creature with power and toughness equal to its mana value.

In the power/toughness setting layer, Starfield of Nyx's effect sets Iroas, God of Victory's power and toughness equal to its mana value.

Amirah gets a single 4/4 white Angel creature token with flying and vigilance instead of the 1/1 red Goblin token, and yes — that Angel token gains haste until end of turn and must attack this combat if able.

Why: Legion Warboss's beginning-of-combat trigger instructs Amirah to create a 1/1 red Goblin creature token. Divine Visitation is a replacement effect that applies to the creation of the token (rule 701.7b: replacement effects on token creation apply before continuous effects that would modify the token's characteristics), so the token is created as a 4/4 white Angel with flying and vigilance instead. Per [Divine Visitation ruling #2], the token's characteristics are entirely replaced — it has no abilities the original Goblin token would have had (the Goblin token had none anyway) — but anything else specified by the effect creating the token still applies. Legion Warboss's clause "That token gains haste until end of turn and attacks this combat if able" is exactly such an extra instruction, so it still applies to the Angel token.

So the Angel token has haste and is required to attack this combat if able. Note the "if able" limit: per [Legion Warboss ruling #2], if the token can't attack (for example, it becomes tapped), it simply doesn't, and if some cost is associated with attacking, Amirah isn't forced to pay it. The Angel token has vigilance, so attacking with it won't tap it.

The token is created untapped and not attacking — Legion Warboss's trigger doesn't put it onto the battlefield attacking, so Amirah declares it as an attacker normally in the declare attackers step. In a multiplayer game this is unchanged: Amirah chooses which defending player, planeswalker, or battle it attacks when attackers are declared; the requirement is only that it attack, not whom it attacks.

No — Dread does not trigger, and it stays in Avianna's graveyard.

Because it triggers on being put into a graveyard "from anywhere" (here, from exile), it is not a leaves-the-battlefield ability and does not "look back in time" — it must trigger from the graveyard itself [603.6c] [603.10a] [Dread ruling #1] [Dread ruling #2]. Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities," so the moment Dread arrives in the graveyard it has no abilities at all, and there is nothing there to trigger [Yixlid Jailer ruling #4] [Dread ruling #0].

- Had the trigger actually occurred (no Yixlid Jailer) and Dread then left the graveyard before resolution, Avianna would still shuffle her library, but Dread would stay in its new zone [701.24c] [Dread ruling #3].
- Ruin Processor's ability moves Dread from exile to its owner's graveyard, so it is Avianna's graveyard even though Niko controls the trigger [Ruin Processor ruling #3].

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more; Yixlid Jailer affects cards in every graveyard, and nothing here depends on player count.
